name: Japan under the shoguns (Kamakura, Muromachi, Sengoku)
summary: Japan from the first warrior government (1185) to the start of the Tokugawa shogunate: the Kamakura and Ashikaga shoguns ruled in the emperor’s name, the Mongols were driven off (1274, 1281), and a century of civil war (the Warring States) ended with unification under Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu.

terrain.value: About 75% mountainous; plains and basins cover about 25%, with the Kantō Plain (Tokyo) the largest.
terrain.source: Library of Congress Country Studies: Japan, geography (checked 9 Nov 2026)

climate.value: Humid and temperate; cool in Hokkaido and subtropical in Kyushu; five or six typhoons pass near Japan each year.
climate.source: Library of Congress Country Studies: Japan, climate (checked 9 Nov 2026)

resources.source: Britannica: shoen; UNESCO: Iwami Ginzan Silver Mine (checked 9 Nov 2026)

disasters.value: Typhoons (the “divine winds”) wrecked Mongol invasion fleets in 1274 and 1281.

population.value: About 5.5–6.3 million in 1150 and 15–17 million in 1600 (Farris); Kitō’s series gives 6.9 million (1150) and 12.3 million (1600). Figures exclude Hokkaido and the Ryukyu chain.
population.source: Farris, Japan’s Medieval Population (2006), Table E.1 and Table I.1 (checked 9 Nov 2026)

urbanisation.value: Kamakura (shogunate headquarters from 1192); Kyoto (imperial court and Ashikaga-era arts); Sakai (a port).
urbanisation.source: Britannica: Minamoto Yoritomo; Ashikaga Yoshimitsu; Sakai (checked 9 Nov 2026)

disease.value: Killer infections, famine and war are the main causes of mortality; epidemics kept population nearly flat before 1150.
disease.source: Farris, Japan’s Medieval Population (2006), Epilogue, p. 264 (checked 9 Nov 2026)

economicBase.value: Rice farming on estates (shōen), where warrior landlords gained control of the land.

tradeRoutes.value: Merchants at the port of Sakai traded with China, Korea, the Ryukyu Islands and Europe (mid-14th to mid-17th century).

wealth.value: Silver mining at Iwami boomed in the 16th and 17th centuries.
wealth.source: UNESCO: Iwami Ginzan Silver Mine and its Cultural Landscape (checked 9 Nov 2026)

moneyAndTax.value: Copper coins from Song China circulated in markets; bills of exchange were used for payments to distant places.
moneyAndTax.source: Britannica: Japan, samurai groups and farming villages (checked 9 Nov 2026)

inequality.value: Samurai and estate lords above farmers; the lowest peasants were called genin.
inequality.source: Britannica: Samurai groups and farming villages (checked 9 Nov 2026)

governmentType.value: The emperor stayed at the imperial court; the shogunate (bakufu) ran military government beside it.

keyRulers.value: Minamoto no Yoritomo. Ashikaga Takauji. Oda Nobunaga. Toyotomi Hideyoshi.
keyRulers.source: Britannica: Minamoto Yoritomo; Ashikaga family; Oda Nobunaga summary; Toyotomi Hideyoshi summary (checked 9 Nov 2026)

succession.value: Shogunal families; Hōjō regents ruled for Kamakura.
succession.source: Britannica: Kamakura period; Hōjō Yasutoki (checked 9 Nov 2026)

institutions.value: Jōei Shikimoku law code (1232), setting out inheritance rules, a new land system and standards for fair trials.

stability.value: Ōnin War (1467–77) led into the Age of Warring States (Sengoku).

armyAndTech.value: Samurai cavalry and archers; matchlock musketeers by 1575 (Oda Nobunaga’s 3,000 at Nagashino).

majorWars.value: Mongol invasions (1274, 1281); Sengoku wars; Hideyoshi’s invasions of Korea (1592 and 1597).
majorWars.source: Britannica: Kamikaze of 1274 and 1281; Toyotomi Hideyoshi (checked 9 Nov 2026)

territoryChange.value: Unified under Toyotomi Hideyoshi’s alliance of daimyo by 1590.

alliancesRivals.value: Formal trade relations with Ming China and Korea; Mongol invasions in 1274 and 1281.
alliancesRivals.source: Britannica: Japan, Muromachi (Ashikaga) period; Kamikaze of 1274 and 1281 (checked 9 Nov 2026)

openness.value: Traded abroad through ports such as Sakai, with China, Korea, the Ryukyu Islands and Europe.

religion.value: Buddhism, including Rinzai Zen (introduced by Eisai in 1191), and Shinto, which blended with Buddhism (shinbutsu shūgō).

languageWriting.value: Written with kanji (Chinese characters) and two kana syllabaries, hiragana and katakana, both derived from Chinese characters.

artsArchitecture.value: Noh theatre and the tea ceremony, promoted by Ashikaga Yoshimasa (Higashiyama culture).

socialStructure.value: Samurai, farmers, artisans attached to estates, and merchants with guilds; the imperial court stood beside the shogunate.
socialStructure.source: Britannica: Samurai groups and farming villages; Kamakura period (checked 9 Nov 2026)

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the dynasty and faith.

neighbours.value: Korea, Ming China, the Ryukyu Islands and the Ainu of Hokkaido.
neighbours.source: Britannica: Sakai; Ainu; Ashikaga period (checked 9 Nov 2026)

ideasReligions.value: Rinzai Zen Buddhism, brought by Eisai in 1191 and patronised by lords and warriors.

riseSignals.value: Minamoto no Yoritomo takes the title of shogun (1192).

peakPeriod.value: Higashiyama culture flourished under Ashikaga Yoshimasa, shogun from 1449.

sources.value: Britannica, UNESCO and Library of Congress pages, listed per item.
sources.source: Britannica; UNESCO; Library of Congress Country Studies (checked 9 Nov 2026)

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles; population figures are estimates.
